identity.name: Rook & Rye
identity.origin: The fictional canal town of Marrowick
identity.nameMeaning: Rook names the clever black birds around the old grain yard; rye names the grain that gives the bakery its darker, patient character.

essence.oneLine: Rook & Rye makes daily bread feel local, useful and worth crossing the street for.
essence.promise: Every loaf has a named grain, a clear bake time and a reason to be on today's shelf.
essence.tension: Dark, inky craft marks meet the soft warmth and slight disorder of a working bakery.

worldview.belief: Good bread belongs to ordinary days, and people deserve to know what is in it, when it was baked and who made it.
worldview.future: A neighbourhood bakery can be both a daily utility and a place where grain, time and labour remain visible.
worldview.humanRole: Bakers judge fermentation, shape dough and explain what changed from one batch to the next.
worldview.technologyRole: Technology records batches, allergens and demand without replacing touch, smell or the baker's judgement.
politicalOrSocialBoundaries: Do not turn the brand into a party-political position.
Do not use anxiety, shame or social status as sales pressure.
Do not romanticise labour or hide who performs it.

purpose.why: Daily food should carry a visible relationship to place, grain and labour.
purpose.mission: Bake a small, useful range each day and explain it without ceremony.
purpose.vision: Neighbourhood bread becomes more transparent, less wasteful and more connected to regional grain.

positioning.category: Neighbourhood bakery, bread subscription and grain workshops
positioning.audience: People who buy bread for everyday meals, nearby cafés and curious home bakers
positioning.need: Fresh bread with known ingredients and reliable collection times, without boutique food theatre.
positioning.difference: A short daily range, visible batch notes and practical grain workshops connect the shelf to the work behind it.
proof: Each fictional loaf card names grain, mill, bake time and allergens.
The fictional batch board records what sold, remained and was repurposed.
positioning.pricePosition: Above supermarket bread, below occasion-led luxury baking; prices reflect regional grain and skilled labour.

offers.name: Daily shelf
offers.job: Put useful bread and two seasonal extras within an easy walk.
offers.outcome: Customers can choose quickly from a short range with clear ingredients and bake times.
proof: Fictional batch cards accompany every item.

offers.name: Saturday grain table
offers.job: Help home bakers understand one grain and one technique through practice.
offers.outcome: A small group leaves with a baked loaf, a repeatable method and honest failure notes.
proof: The fictional workshop uses one shared dough at different fermentation stages.

audiences.name: The daily neighbour
audiences.context: They are collecting food on the way home and have little time for explanation.
audiences.job: Choose a loaf that fits dinner and dietary needs in under a minute.
audiences.desiredShift: From 'Which expensive loaf am I meant to understand?' to 'I know what this is for tonight.'
audiences.language: Plain names, ingredients and practical serving notes.

audiences.name: The curious home baker
audiences.context: They can follow a recipe but struggle to read fermentation and grain behaviour.
audiences.job: Learn one physical cue they can repeat at home.
audiences.desiredShift: From copying times to noticing dough.
audiences.language: Sensory verbs and precise ranges, never mystical craft language.

values.name: Daily usefulness
values.meaning: Bread earns its place at breakfast, in a lunch bag and beside soup.
antiBehaviours: display food that is impractical to eat

values.name: Visible grain
values.meaning: Ingredients, origin and variation stay legible.

messaging.masterMessage: Today’s bread, what it is for, and when it came out of the oven.

messagePillars.name: Today
messagePillars.claim: The range follows today's batch, not an endless menu.

messagePillars.name: Known grain
messagePillars.claim: Every loaf names its grain and mill.

messagePillars.name: Useful knowledge
messagePillars.claim: Workshops teach cues people can repeat at home.

messaging.storyPattern: Open with the day and the loaf. Show grain, hands and time. End with the meal or skill it makes possible.

dimensions.instruction: Name the bread's job before describing atmosphere.
Allow human rhythm and a little flour on the sentence.
Use smell, crust, crumb and touch, then give the useful number.

avoid: claims with no physical or recorded proof

do: give an owner and next update
say what happened and what remains safe
avoid: jokes during loss or payment issues

language.defaultRegister: Everyday British English. Friendly without pet names, foodie performance or heritage cosplay.
language.sentenceRhythm: Short notices and one longer sensory sentence. Sound like a person behind the counter, not a lifestyle magazine.

terminology.product: loaf, bun or pastry by its plain name
terminology.provenance: name the actual farm or mill

formatting: lists only when they improve scanning
language.inclusiveLanguage: Name real roles and actions. Do not invent personal characteristics or reduce an audience to a demographic stereotype.

allowed: This fictional batch was baked today.
This fictional loaf contains the listed grain and allergens.
The grain table is a practical two-hour workshop in this fictional scenario.
forbidden: a certification that does not exist
disclaimers: This is a fictional Brand DNA dataset. No company, product, customer or performance claim is real.

onBrand: Rye tin, 08:10. Dark crust. Built for butter and soup.

offBrand: Elevate your morning with our artisanal masterpieces.
An unforgettable journey through the ancient soul of grain.
Premium baked experiences, handcrafted to perfection.

concept.direction: Ink-black bakery marks, oat paper, kiln red and butter yellow around honest close-up food photography.
concept.rationale: The identity borrows from batch stamps and paper bags, then lets warm bread and working surfaces break the grid.
concept.visualTension: Hard black marks and soft bread; a tidy information grid and a visibly active bench.

usage: Oat and ink carry most of the system.
Kiln red marks what is current or actionable.
Let bread supply the richest colour in photography.

gradients.name: Oven edge
gradients.job: A rare transition on workshop covers

rules: Keep display type compact and sentence case.
Do not simulate vintage distress on live copy.

logo.idea: A rook footprint reduced to three grain-like cuts beside a sturdy wordmark; recognisable as a mark, not a bird illustration.

variants.background: light or dark according to the approved master

logo.clearspace: At least the cap height of the first letter on every side.
placement: align to the primary content grid
keep away from photography focal points
use one-colour variants when contrast is uncertain
dont: use the symbol as a decorative texture

layout.principle: A practical batch ledger interrupted by one generous crop of bread or hands.
layout.grid: Six columns on desktop, four on tablet and one reading column on mobile.
layout.density: Compact for products and times; spacious for stories and workshops.
composition: time and availability lead product cards
labels sit on a strict baseline
allow torn or dusted edges only in photography
responsive: keep the primary action above bottom navigation
allow text to wrap without collision
prove zero horizontal overflow at 390 px

shapes.geometry: Rectangles, ruled ledger lines and one three-cut rook motif.
shapes.corners: 2-4 px on functional controls; paper and image masks may remain square.
shapes.strokes: 1.5 px for UI and 2 px for marks.

iconography.job: Label ingredients, collection, allergens and workshop actions instantly.
iconography.metaphor: Simple objects from the bakery and table, drawn as sturdy stamped outlines.
iconography.grid: 24 × 24 px with a 2 px optical safe area.
iconography.detail: One primary form and no more than one supporting detail; test at 16 px.
iconography.color: One colour by default; kiln red marks only an active or selected state.
opticalRules: open narrow gaps at small sizes
align repeated elements to whole pixels where possible
dont: put the icon in a presentation mockup

illustration.job: Explain grain, fermentation and batch flow when photography cannot show the relationship.
illustration.style: Two-colour cut-paper diagrams with stamped labels added as live type.
illustration.perspective: Flat side view or simple top-down process map.
dont: cute characters without a narrative job

photography.job: Make the viewer understand today's bread, its texture and the work that shaped it.
subjects: one baker at a real task
a customer's meal context without staged joy
photography.moment: The minute bread changes hands: scored, lifted from a rack, torn or wrapped.
composition: negative space for live batch text
photography.camera: Handheld full-frame or APS-C at bench height, slight natural movement.
photography.lens: 35 mm for place, 50-85 mm for hands and crumb; moderate depth of field.
photography.light: Soft morning window light with warm practical oven spill; no golden haze filter.
photography.palette: Oat, ink and crust browns with small kiln-red objects.
photography.grade: Warm highlights, neutral flour whites, deep but open shadows, restrained saturation.
photography.texture: Crumb, paper fibres, worn wood and brushed steel remain tactile.
do: grade a series as one shoot

motion.principle: Movement follows the daily cycle: stamp, slide, tear, wrap and clear.
signature: a batch stamp resolving into live information
a scored line revealing a section
motion.reducedMotion: Replace spatial movement and looping signals with an immediate static state change.
avoid: motion that competes with the task

dataVisualization.principle: Batch, allergens, quantities and waste records must remain plain enough to check.
dataVisualization.colors: Ink and oat as the base, kiln red for current, butter for attention, never colour alone.
rules: never use colour as the only distinction

representation.principle: Show bakers and customers as ordinary skilled people in a working neighbourhood shop, never as rustic characters.

casting.people: One person or a small working pair; customers appear only when their action matters.
casting.age: Adults of varied working ages, roughly 20-70, chosen for the real role.
casting.gender: Balance a series without assigning baking, ownership or care through gender.
casting.ethnicity: Everyday local variety can appear through explicit editorial casting, never inference.
casting.ability: Keep entrances, counters and tasks believable for varied bodies; do not use disability as a story device.
casting.roles: The person doing the skilled action owns the frame.
casting.wardrobe: Washed aprons, T-shirts, knitwear and practical shoes; used, clean and credible.
casting.behaviour: Focused hands, quick exchanges, tasting and checking rather than camera-facing smiles.

representation.sensitiveAttributePolicy: Never infer ethnicity, religion, health, sexual orientation, gender identity or another sensitive attribute from a name, face, place or industry. Unknown remains unknown.
representation.consent: Recognisable real people require documented permission for the exact channel and context. Do not reuse customer or staff imagery as generic campaign material.
avoid: roles assigned through gender or age stereotypes
synthetic faces presented as real staff
children without a necessary context and explicit guardian consent

sensory.sonicIdentity: An early shop waking up: paper, crust, tray and low conversation, never a nostalgic café soundtrack.

voiceover.voice: Close, adult and conversational; regional accent is welcome when genuine.

sensory.silence: Leave room around the first cut of a loaf and the sentence that names its batch.

universal: Keep verified facts, fictional demonstration content, creative decisions and inference visibly separate.
Write Rook & Rye exactly as shown; do not invent variants or sub-brands.
kiln red must have a functional or narrative job.
Use real typography for readable words; image models do not create logos, labels or certificates.
Show people as capable participants, not decoration.
Do not publish a claim that the fictional evidence model would reject.
A production is complete only after its real target size and channel have been checked.

accessibility.standard: WCAG 2.2 AA for digital work; accessible PDF practices for documents.
contrast: Normal text must reach at least 4.5:1.
Large text and interface boundaries must reach at least 3:1.
Colour can never be the only carrier of state.
Use only pairings that have been measured, not guessed from appearance.
motion: Do not autoplay essential information without controls.
Every animated state needs an immediate static equivalent.
text: Keep body copy as selectable, scalable text.
Write links that describe their destination.
Explain specialist terms at first use.
media: Alt text describes the image's communication job.
Decorative images receive empty alt text.
Video includes captions and a transcript.

trademarks: The name is fictional but still requires a real clearance search before commercial adoption.
Never recreate a third-party mark in generated assets.
assets: Record the source and licence for every font, image, icon and sound.
Keep logo masters as vectors outside image-generation prompts.
Do not copy imagery from an unrelated real organisation into this example.
claims: Every public claim needs a real source or owner approval.
Fictional proof cannot be reused as a real testimonial.
Measure environmental, time and performance claims before stating them.
privacy: Do not add personal data that is unnecessary for the artifact.
Use recognisable people only with documented rights.
